title: Encryption & Key Management Review - Omega Finance
summary: Customer asked for detailed proof that Redwood supports customer-managed keys (BYOK) with HSM-backed providers, audit log visibility for key usage, and controls for key access mapping to RBAC/SSO. Discussion covered envelope encryption, CMKs vs data keys, exportability limitations, rotation policies, and options for Dedicated/Private deployments.
next_steps: Share SOC2/ISO attestations and KMS controls snapshot
Schedule follow-up technical deep dive with Omega infra team (w/ CloudHSM engineer)
Provide sample audit log extract and sample IAM policy mapping
action_items: Maya Chen: Share BYOK integration whitepaper and sample CloudHSM diagram by 2025-03-14
Rafael Ortiz: Prepare small demo env showing envelope encryption and audit logs by 2025-03-21
Priya Kapoor: Pull SOC2 encryption control section and redact PII, share by 2025-03-13
Nina Patel (Omega): Confirm preferred KMS provider (AWS CloudHSM vs Google HSM) by 2025-03-18
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Rafael Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood Security), Liam O'Connor (Omega Head of Security), Nina Patel (Omega Cloud Infra), Jorge Morales (Omega Compliance)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, imperfect): Customer needs BYOK with HSM, wants key usage logs, RBAC mapping to SSO, and confirmation about data residency.

[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Liam: Hey, Liam here.
[00:10] Nina: Nina here.
[00:12] Jorge: Jorge.
[00:14] Maya: Great. Rafael and Priya on our side?
[00:16] Rafael: Rafael, yep.
[00:18] Priya: Priya, hi.
[00:21] Maya: Thanks. The agenda is encryption at rest and in transit, KMS options including BYOK and HSM, audit logging for key usage, and how RBAC/SSO maps to key access. We'll leave time for Q&A.

[02:05] Liam: To start high level — Omega runs regulated financial workloads. We need customer-controlled keys for any persistent PII-derived embeddings or extractable artifacts. SOC 2 will want us to prove key custody. Can Redwood support BYOK with HSM-backed keys?

[02:25] Rafael: Short answer, yes. We support customer-managed keys via envelope encryption. Let me unpack: Redwood never stores plaintext model artifacts; we persist encrypted blobs. We leverage a data-key (DEK) per logical object, encrypted with a customer CMK in your KMS — which can be an HSM-backed CMK.

[02:50] Nina: When you say CMK, are you talking about a customer master key that you call across requests? Does Redwood ever have the ability to export that CMK?

[03:02] Priya: Important clarification — our architecture uses CMKs as non-exportable root keys. We do not export primary keys. We use envelope encryption: ephemeral data keys are generated and wrapped with your CMK. That means Redwood only stores the wrapped DEKs and cannot decrypt without calling your KMS to unwrap.

[03:26] Jorge: And key rotation? We have a policy to rotate keys quarterly and retain ability to decrypt older data. How do we handle key rotation and backward-compat?

[03:40] Rafael: We support key rotation via versioned CMKs and we keep key metadata so wrapped DEKs indicate which CMK version they were encrypted under. When you rotate the CMK in your KMS, you keep the old key for decrypt operations as required. Our docs show recommended rotation patterns — rotate the CMK, then re-wrap DEKs as part of a background job if you need to proactively re-encrypt.

[04:10] Liam: Are there latency implications? Every decrypt requires a KMS call, right? For inference path that could add ms. We need a sense of p50/p95 impact.

[04:22] Rafael: Correct, unwrap is a KMS API call. We mitigates with caching of unwrapped DEKs in an encrypted, ephemeral process memory (not persisted to disk), bounded TTLs, and in Dedicated/Private deployments we can localize the KMS endpoint to the same VPC to keep latency low. In our internal benchmarks, KMS unwrap adds ~5-20ms depending on region and provider. But real impact depends on how often you create new DEKs; for model serving we reuse DEKs for session scoped artifacts and rely on prefix/KV cache to avoid repeating unwraps on every token.

[05:05] Nina: If we want absolute isolation — we plan to use a VPC Private deployment where our KMS is in our VPC. Can Redwood call our KMS endpoints across peered network?

[05:18] Priya: Yes, Private and Dedicated support connecting to your KMS via VPC peering or PrivateLink. For on-prem or air-gapped customers we support on-prem HSMs as well, though that setup is a custom engagement.

[05:35] Jorge: Let's talk HSM specifics. We use AWS CloudHSM for root key material. Does Redwood support CloudHSM-based CMKs? Can you sign or unwrap inside CloudHSM?

[05:47] Rafael: We integrate with cloud KMS providers (AWS KMS backed by CloudHSM, GCP KMS with CMEK/HSM, Azure Key Vault HSM) and with customer-owned CloudHSM in private deployments. Important note: if you use AWS KMS with AWS CloudHSM backing managed by AWS, the CMK is non-exportable. For private CloudHSM where you hold the cluster, our service can call your HSM via an API gateway in the VPC. In most cases unwrap/sign operations are performed inside the KMS/HSM boundary — Redwood never imports raw key material.

[06:21] Liam: Good. For our auditors we need to show key usage logs tied to user identities — who requested an unwrap, from which host, and why. Does Redwood surface KMS audit logs, or do we have to pull them from the cloud provider?

[06:36] Priya: We provide a few options. If using your cloud KMS, you will have cloud provider logs (CloudTrail, Audit Logs) that show KMS API calls and caller identity. Redwood also emits our own audit events in the Control Plane — we log each high-level operation (e.g., model decrypt attempt, key wrap operation) with request IDs and routing info. We can correlate Redwood audit events with provider KMS logs if you share correlation IDs.

[07:02] Nina: Are those Redwood audit logs tamper-evident? Retention? Exportable to our SIEM?

[07:09] Priya: Logs are stored with integrity checks in the Control Plane; for Dedicated/Private we can forward logs to your SIEM via secure syslog or CloudWatch/Log Sink. Retention policies are configurable per contract — we can keep a shorter window on hosted and longer for enterprise packages.

[07:30] Liam: Mapping of RBAC/SSO — we want that a decryption must be approved by a role that maps to a SAML group. Can Redwood enforce per-key access policy tied to SSO groups?

[07:44] Rafael: On the application side, our RBAC layer in the Redwood Console controls which identities can request certain API operations. For KMS calls where your KMS handles policy, we recommend combining provider-side IAM policies (so only Redwood service principals from your account/VPC can call the CMK) plus Redwood-level RBAC that gates who within your org can trigger operations that cause decrypts. So it's a two-layer model: provider IAM for service-to-KMS trust and Redwood Console RBAC for human/operator access.

[08:18] Jorge: Sounds fine. We will need evidence for SOC 2 that access changes are auditable. How do you handle RBAC changes and SSO provisioning events?

[08:27] Priya: We log admin changes, role assignments, and SSO provisioning events. If you use SAML/SCIM to provision groups, each SCIM event and the resulting role mapping are recorded. We can provide an exportable CSV of role changes for audit purposes.

[08:45] Nina: A specific question about encryption in transit — do you support TLS 1.2+ with client certificates and mutual TLS for service-to-service communication?

[08:54] Rafael: Yes. All network traffic is TLS 1.2+ (we recommend TLS 1.3). For private links between Redwood and customer KMS or private endpoints we support mTLS and IP allow lists.

[09:08] Liam: If we require a split-key model or dual control — e.g., two operators must sign to unwrap a critical key — can Redwood accommodate that?

[09:18] Priya: That’s a more advanced control. At the KMS-level some HSMs support quorum or multi-party authorization. Redwood can respect that as long as the KMS presents that API. On the Redwood side we can implement an approval workflow that prevents a decryption operation from proceeding until an approval is registered. This would be an enterprise feature and likely require a Dedicated/Private deployment and product engineering time.

[09:48] Nina: About data residency — we need keys and decrypted material to stay in EMEA. We operate strict controls. Can Redwood guarantee that with a private deployment?

[09:59] Rafael: Yes, Private deployments with regional control ensure data and key material stay in customer-selected regions. For hosted customers we provide region pinning and can isolate keys to a specific provider region but legal guarantees are stronger in Private deployments where compute and control plane sit in your VPC.

[10:20] Liam: Compliance attestations — will you provide SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 documents?

[10:26] Priya: We can share SOC 2 and ISO summaries and a CA-signed attestation under NDA. We'll send redacted reports and a control matrix that maps encryption controls to our policies.

[10:37] Jorge: One more technical: when you say "wrapped DEKs in storage" — are these stored per-object, or per-bucket, or per-tenant? We need granularity to ensure least-privilege of decrypts.

[10:50] Rafael: We associate a DEK per logical object (e.g., dataset or model snapshot) and metadata includes tenant ID and required roles. That allows us to restrict which service paths can request unwrapping. On multi-tenant hosted plans we enforce strict tenant isolation; on Dedicated the tenancy lines are clearer.

[11:15] Maya: Quick pause, I want to surface a common misunderstanding. Some customers think BYOK means Redwood can never call the KMS. That's not the case — Redwood needs call-out rights to perform unwrap/wrap for operations, but the CMK remains under your control and non-exportable. If you want to fully control every key operation, that maps to a flow where you intercept or approve unwraps — which is doable but more manual.

[11:40] Liam: Understood. For the audit, we'll want a demo showing end-to-end: object encrypted, DEK wrapped by our CMK, call trace in Redwood logs, and matching CloudTrail entry. Can you show that?

[11:53] Rafael: Yes. That's one of the follow-up deliverables — we can provision a demo in a sandbox account with your KMS and show the correlation.

[12:05] Nina: There are occasionally transcription-thing: in the docs sometimes K V cache is spelled as K V or KV — just flagging we want the exact terminology in the whitepaper.

[12:15] Maya: Good call. We'll standardize terms.

[12:22] Jorge: A commercial/contract question — if we bring our own key and we terminate, can we demand key destruction and artifacts securely wiped?

[12:31] Priya: Yes. When the contract ends we support key revocation processes and secure wiping of wrapped DEKs and any ephemeral caches. For hosted customers we can coordinate with your legal/infosec to provide a certificate of destruction. For Dedicated/Private, since keys are in your KMS, destruction is under your control.

[12:52] Liam: What about backup/export? If you keep wrapped DEKs in backups, we need guarantees about how backups are encrypted and where they reside.

[13:04] Rafael: Backups are encrypted — wrapped DEKs remain wrapped and backups are stored in regioned object stores. We can provide backup encryption metadata and export controls.

[13:18] Nina: One more — what pivot controls do you have for privileged Redwood engineers? For example, can a Redwood SRE request a decrypt in emergencies? How is that authorized and audited?

[13:30] Priya: Privileged access is tightly controlled: we have a just-in-time access workflow, approval gates, and SSO-based audit trails. Emergency decrypts require approval and are logged with reason, approver, and time. Those records are available for audits.

[13:50] Liam: Great. Let's surface a few specific test criteria for our security checklist — we will run a short POC where we: 1) create a CMK in our account 2) configure Redwood to use it 3) store a model snapshot and verify wrapped DEK in storage 4) trigger a decrypt and show logs 5) rotate the CMK and show we can still decrypt old objects. Does that align?

[14:15] Rafael: That's perfect. We also suggest adding a stress test to measure p95 latency during burst traffic when unwrap TTLs expire.

[14:30] Jorge: One small ask — include a sample IAM policy snippet that limits KMS decrypt to Redwood’s service principal scoped to our account/VPC. That will speed our infra team's review.

[14:40] Maya: We'll include that in the materials.

[14:45] Liam: Any blockers on Redwood's side for doing BYOK with CloudHSM?

[14:51] Rafael: No blockers — only implementation details and network setup. For managed KMS (AWS KMS backed by CloudHSM) it's straightforward. For customer-owned HSM, we'll need a connectivity plan.

[15:05] Nina: Timeline wise, if we want to start a pilot in mid-April, is that feasible?

[15:12] Maya: Feasible. We'll aim to deliver docs by Mar 14, demo by Mar 21, and target provisioning for pilot the week of Apr 14.

[15:24] Jorge: Sounds good. Quick note — our compliance team will want to review the Redwood key lifecycle diagram; please annotate where key material enters/exits and which components are in our control.

[15:36] Priya: Will do.

[15:40] Maya: OK, let's capture next steps. I'll send the BYOK whitepaper and CloudHSM diagram, Rafael will prepare demo env, Priya will share SOC2 snippets, and we'll schedule the deep dive.

[15:53] Liam: Thanks everyone.
[15:55] Nina: Thanks.
[15:56] Maya: Meeting adjourned.
